authoredPrompt: This figure is a compact three-dimensional vector diagram drawn on a set of coordinate axes. The z-axis rises vertically, the y-axis extends to the right, and the x-axis runs toward the lower left, out of the page; all three are thin black lines with small arrowheads and italic labels, meeting at an unlabeled origin. Two purple dots mark positions in space, P_1 sitting above and to the right of the origin and P_2 lower and farther to the right. A thick purple arrow from the origin to P_1 is labeled r(t_1) and a second purple arrow from the origin to P_2 is labeled r(t_2), both symbols carrying overhead vector arrows. A third purple arrow of the same weight runs directly from P_1 to P_2 and is labeled delta r. The three arrows close into a triangle, so the picture shows the displacement as exactly the vector that must be added to the earlier position vector to arrive at the later one. Casting the difference of two position vectors as a single arrow drawn between the two points extends the one-dimensional idea of displacement to motion anywhere in space.
authoredInteractions:
- Drag point P1 or P2: learner moves either endpoint in 3D space; r(t1), r(t2), and delta r redraw immediately while the triangle relation closes; the vector difference delta r = r(t2) - r(t1) becomes visible as the arrow between positions.
- Button sequence from initial position to final position: learner steps from origin-to-P1, then origin-to-P2, then P1-to-P2; each vector appears in order; the displacement is understood as the change needed to carry the earlier position vector to the later one.
authoredContext:
With our definition of the position of a particle in three-dimensional space, we can formulate the three-dimensional displacement. The figure shows a particle at time t1 located at P1 with position vector r→(t1). At a later time t2, the particle is located at P2 with position vector r→(t2). The displacement vector Δr→ is found by subtracting r→(t1) from r→(t2):

Vector addition is discussed in Vectors. Note that this is the same operation we did in one dimension, but now the vectors are in three-dimensional space.

The displacement Δr→=r→(t2)−r→(t1) is the vector from P1 to P2.

An x y z coordinate system is shown, with positive x out of the page, positive y to the right, and positive z up. Two points, P 1 and P 2 are shown. The vector r of t 1 from the origin to P 1 and the vector r of t 2 from the origin to P 2 are shown as purple arrows. The vector delta r is shown as a purple arrow whose tail is at P 1 and head at P 2.

The following examples illustrate the concept of displacement in multiple dimensions.

discrepancies: Default view shows only the axes and bare points; the three purple vectors r(t1), r(t2), and Δr — the entire content of the source figure — are hidden until the user presses a button
The combining arrow accent (r⃗) renders as tofu/missing-glyph boxes in the panel header and likely in the vector labels, unlike the clean harpoon/arrow notation in the source
Points P1 and P2 are large purple spheres, whereas the source shows them as small dots at the arrow tips
In the source P1 sits higher and Δr descends steeply to P2; the generated default placement makes the triangle proportions somewhat different (P2 quite close to the y-axis region)
evaluation.notes: Geometry, camera orientation, and the vector-triangle concept (including drag and step-through interactions) are correct, but the default view hides all three vectors behind a button press and the r⃗ combining-arrow glyph renders as tofu, weakening at-a-glance fidelity to the source.
action_items: Show all three vectors and their labels by default; let the step-through button rebuild them progressively instead of starting from an empty figure
Replace the combining arrow character (r⃗) with an image/SVG overline, a 'vec' styled span, or plain 'Δr / r(t1)' text so labels do not show missing-glyph boxes
Shrink the P1/P2 spheres to small dots matching the source's point markers
